new_groups.label: Mr. Breckenridge's speech in the Senate, 8 January 1802, on his motion to repeal the judiciary act of 1801
new_groups.definition: Printings of the speech with which Mr. Breckenridge, senator from Kentucky, opened the Senate's debate of 8 January 1802 on his resolution to repeal the act of the last session 'for a new organization of the Judiciary System' (the act of 13 February 1801, which had created sixteen circuit judges): 'It will be expected of me, I presume, Sir, as I introduced the resolution now under consideration, to assign my reasons for wishing a repeal of this law. This I shall do; and shall endeavour to shew, 1. That the law is unnecessary and improper, and was so at its passage'. Most papers print it under the heading 'Judiciary Establishment', from the National Intelligencer's report of the Senate's debates. A senator's own argument, as the papers reported the debate.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The American consul at Havana's circular of 25 December 1801: the ports of Cuba closed to American and all foreign vessels
new_groups.definition: Printings of a circular dated 'American Consulate, Havanna, December 25, 1801' and signed by the consul of the United States there: 'By an order of the government of this island, published this day, the admission of American, and all other foreign vessels into its ports, is prohibited from this date. You will be pleased, Sir, to give immediate publicity to this information, for the government of the merchants and traders of your district.' The papers print copies sent to the collectors of different ports (Baltimore, Philadelphia, New York); the Oracle's adds a postscript of 31 December. The American consul's own notice of a Spanish colonial order.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Baltimore, January 1802: a letter from Alexandria reports that Toussaint 'is no more'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph from the Baltimore Federal Gazette of 23 January 1802, headed 'Death of Toussaint' or 'Important' in several papers: 'A gentleman belonging to a respectable mercantile house of Alexandria, now in this town, received a letter from his partner last night, dated the 21st inst. which says, "I am sorry to inform you Toussaint is no more. He has been caught by the blacks and burnt alive."' The Baltimore paper adds that the same report was current at Norfolk, 'tho' not generally credited', and gives its own guesses at how it happened. A report at third hand of a rumour; the papers of the following months print Toussaint as alive (his arrest in June is the story of Leclerc's proclamation, below).
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The French army arrives at St. Domingo, February 1802: the Consuls' proclamation and a report of the burning of the Cape
new_groups.definition: Two items of March 1802 on the French expedition under General Leclerc, which reached St. Domingo (Saint-Domingue, now Haiti) early in February: the proclamation of the Consuls of the French Republic to the inhabitants of the island, which Leclerc published on landing, and a Baltimore report, from a ship's captain, of the burning of Cape François. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Consuls of the French Republic to the inhabitants of St. Domingo, 8 November 1801: 'Whatever may be your origin and your colour, you are all Frenchmen'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the proclamation of the Consuls of the Republic dated Paris, 17 Brumaire, year 10 (8 November 1801), which General Leclerc published at St. Domingo in February 1802: 'Inhabitants of St. Domingo, Whatever may be your origin and your colour, you are all Frenchmen, you are all free and all equal before God and the Republic. France, like St. Domingo, has been a prey to factions'; it announces the Captain General sent with the army and warns those who would not rally to him. The papers print it in two translations: four that begin 'Inhabitants of St. Domingo, Whatever may be your origin, and your colour, you are all Frenchmen' and go on 'But an entire change has taken place', and three that read 'ye are all Frenchmen, ye are all free' and 'But all is changed'; counted together as one item in two printed forms. Several papers print it after Leclerc's own short proclamation, which is not counted here (5 papers). The French government's own proclamation, as the papers translated it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Baltimore, March 1802: 'Conflagration of the Cape', from the captain of the schooner Nelly
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report from Baltimore, dated 3 March 1802 in some papers and 4 March in others, headed 'Conflagration of the Cape' in most: 'Arrived last evening, capt. Rogers of the Schooner Nelly, from Cape-Francois, which he left on the 14th February. The news by capt. R. is most distressing; both on account of the American property which has been destroyed at the Cape, and the scenes of horror and bloodshed which have and will take place.' It goes on, in the Baltimore paper's words, with the arrival of the French fleet off the Cape on 3 February, the negotiations, the firing of the town on the night of the 4th and the killings that followed. A ship captain's report at second hand, in the Baltimore paper's words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The act of 16 March 1802 fixing the military peace establishment of the United States
new_groups.definition: Printings, among the laws of the first session of the Seventh Congress, of 'An Act Fixing the military peace establishment of the United States': 'That the military peace establishment of the United States, from and after the first of June next, shall be composed of one regiment of artillerists and two regiments of infantry, with such officers, military agents, and engineers, as are hereinafter mentioned'. Among its sections, the President is empowered to organise a corps of engineers, which 'shall be stationed at West Point in the State of New-York, and shall constitute a military academy'. Congress's own act, printed 'By Authority'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The treaty signed at Madrid on 21 March 1801 by Lucien Bonaparte and the Prince of Peace, printed in 1802 as proof that 'Spain has ceded Louisiana to the French'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a treaty 'Signed at Madrid, 21st March, 1801, by the Prince of Peace and Lucien Bonaparte' (the dates vary from paper to paper), from the Paris Journal des Débats of January 1802: 'The First Consul of the French republic and his Catholic Majesty, desirous of permanently determining the states which the son of the Infant of Parma shall receive, as an equivalent for the Duchy of Parma, have agreed to the following articles'; the Grand Duchy of Tuscany is given to the Prince of Parma, who will be acknowledged King of Tuscany. The National Intelligencer's headnote, which most papers repeat, says that the document 'establishes the fact, that Spain has ceded Louisiana to the French'. The two governments' treaty, as a Paris paper gave it, with the American paper's headnote.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The definitive treaty of peace signed at Amiens, 27 March 1802
new_groups.definition: Printings of the text of the 'Definitive Treaty of Peace, between the French Republic, the King of Spain, and the Batavian Republic, on the one part, and His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great-Britain and Ireland on the other', signed at Amiens on 27 March 1802 and brought to America in May from London and Havre papers: 'The First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French Nation, and His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great-Britain and Ireland, being equally animated with a desire to put an end to the calamities of war'. Among its articles, Spain cedes the island of Trinidad and the Batavian Republic its possessions in Ceylon to Great Britain, and Malta is to be restored to the Knights of St. John. The powers' own treaty, as the papers printed it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Leclerc to the citizens of St. Domingo, June 1802: 'I have thought proper to cause him to be arrested'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the proclamation of the French general in chief at St. Domingo, dated at the Cape, 20 Prairial, year 10 (8 June 1802), and signed by Leclerc, in two translations. Six papers print the one that begins 'General Toussaint not being contented with enjoying the amnesty which had been granted him, attempted again to kindle the flames of civil war. I have thought proper to cause him to be arrested'; three print another: 'Gen. Toussaint did not wish to enjoy the amnesty which had been granted to him; he has continued to conspire; he was just going to rekindle a civil war. I thought it necessary to have him arrested'. Both promise that the proofs will be published and that the measure should not alarm those who have laid down their arms. Counted together as one item in two printed forms. The French commander's own proclamation, as the papers translated it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New York, July 1802: from Captain Dawson, 'an engagement between two Algerine cruisers and a Portuguese man of war off Malaga'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report from the New York Gazette of 16 July 1802, from the captain of a schooner arrived in 38 days from Gibraltar: 'From Capt. Dawson we have received an account of an engagement between two Algerine cruisers and a Portuguese man of war off Malaga, wherein the former were victorious. The force of the Algerines was a frigate of 32 guns (the same which was presented by the American government to the Dey) and a xebec'; the Portuguese frigate struck after an action of three hours and was carried into Algiers. The Virginia Argus prints a Philadelphia form of the report that opens in other words ('The Captain of an American vessel arrived at New-York from Gibraltar, has given an account of the engagement') and goes on in the same words; counted with the others as a printed form. A ship captain's report at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Thomas Paine returns to America, 1802: the President's letter to him, and his letters 'To the Citizens of the United States'
new_groups.definition: Three documents on the return of Thomas Paine, author of 'Common Sense' and 'The Rights of Man', who had lived in Europe since 1787 and landed at Baltimore at the end of October 1802: the President's letter of 1801 offering him a passage in a national ship, published in August 1802 from a London paper, and the first two of Paine's letters 'To the Citizens of the United States', which the National Intelligencer published in November. Contains those three groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: 'You expressed a wish in your letter to return to America by a national ship': the President's letter to Thomas Paine, published August 1802
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter from Thomas Jefferson, President of the United States, to Thomas Paine, which a New York paper took from a London paper in August 1802 ('about which so much has been said'): 'You expressed a wish in your letter to return to America by a national ship; Mr. Dawson, who brings over the treaty, and who will present you this letter, is charged with orders to the Captain of the Maryland to receive and accommodate you back, if you can be ready to depart at such a short warning'; it ends with the wish that Paine 'may long live to continue your useful labours, and to reap their reward in the thankfulness of nations'. Papers of both parties printed it, some with hostile introductions; two printed it again in essays and columns of the President's letters. The President's own letter, as the papers printed it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Thomas Paine, 'To the Citizens of the United States', Letter the First: 'After an absence of almost fifteen years, I am again returned'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the first of Thomas Paine's letters 'To the Citizens of the United States', first published in the National Intelligencer of 15 November 1802: 'After an absence of almost fifteen years, I am again returned to the country in whose dangers I bore my share, and to whose greatness I contributed my part. When I sailed for Europe in the spring of 1787 it was my intention to return to America the next year'. He quotes a letter of his own of about 1789 on the principles of the revolution 'expiring on the soil that produced them', and closes by declaring 'the line of conduct I shall pursue'. Papers of both parties printed it, some with introductions for or against him. Paine's own public letter, a political argument.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Thomas Paine, 'To the Citizens of the United States', Letter the Second: on the ex-president John Adams and the Federalists
new_groups.definition: Printings of the second of Thomas Paine's letters 'To the Citizens of the United States', first published in the National Intelligencer of 22 November 1802: 'As the affairs of the country to which I am returned are of more importance to the world, and to me, than of that I have lately left (for it is through the new world the old must be regenerated, if regenerated at all) I shall not take up the subject of the French revolution'. It turns on 'the ex-president John Adams', whom it accuses, in Paine's words, of having projects 'to overturn the liberties of America, and the representative system of government'. Paine's own public letter: a political argument with allegations against a named public man.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Paris, August 1802: the president of the Conservative Senate addresses Bonaparte, proclaimed First Consul for life, and the First Consul replies
new_groups.definition: Printings of the account from the Paris papers of 3 and 4 August 1802, in two translations, of the Conservative Senate's audience with the First Consul: its president, Barthélemy, 'addressed Bonaparte in a speech of which the following are extracts: "Citizen First Consul, The French, grateful for the immense services you have rendered to them, wish that the First Magistracy of the State should be irrevocably placed in your hands"' ('A new career commences for the First Consul'), read the Senate's decree that, as the papers print it, 3,568,885 of 3,577,259 citizens had voted for Napoleon Bonaparte as Consul for life, and the First Consul replied. Five papers print the translation that begins 'At the Levee yesterday'; three print another ('The French people, as a mark of gratitude'), which the Alexandria Advertiser takes from the New York Mercantile Advertiser. Counted together as one item in two printed forms. The French Senate's and the First Consul's own words, as the papers translated them.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Washington, 13 October 1802: 'letters have been received in this country from Algiers, as late as the 7th of July'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph from Washington of 13 October 1802: 'We understand that letters have been received in this country from Algiers, as late as the 7th of July, which furnish the following information: The Dey of Algiers has demanded of the American Consul to direct the United States frigate the George Washington, to be brought to Algiers, for the purpose of being sent by the Dey to Constantinople'; the Dey later turned to the consuls of nearer nations; a Tripolitan corsair brought the American brig Franklin into Algiers as a prize; Spain bought off a threatened war. A report at second hand, from letters the paragraph does not name.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Madrid, August 1802: 'the plenipotentiaries of the United States and Spain signed a convention' for a board of commissioners on losses
new_groups.definition: Printings of a short letter from Madrid dated in August 1802 (15 August in most papers), which some papers call a circular of the American consul general at Madrid and others a letter 'from an official character at the Spanish court': 'On the 11th instant the plenipotentiaries of the United States and Spain signed a convention for the appointment of commissioners who are to form a board, and sit at Madrid, for the indemnification of those who have sustained losses, damages, or injuries in consequence of the excesses of individuals of either nation, during the late war, contrary to the existing treaty or the law of nations. The convention to have no force or effect, until it be ratified by the contracting parties.' An official's letter, as the papers printed it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New York, 3 November 1802: 'one of the most alarming Fires that has ever happened in this city'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York report of 3 November 1802, in two forms: 'One of the most alarming Fires that has ever happened in this city, within our recollection, broke out last evening, between 8 & 9 o'clock, in a stable in Bridge-street, between Whitehall & Broad-streets' (two papers), or 'Last evening one of the most alarming Fires that has ever happened in this city, broke out in a stable in Bride-street, between Whitehall and Broad-streets' (five papers; the street is printed 'Bride-street' in some papers and 'Bridge-street' in others); in less than an hour and a half about fifty buildings, mostly dwelling houses, were burnt, pulled down or gutted. The report goes on to name some of the sufferers; the excerpts end before their names. Counted together as one report in two printed forms. A New York paper's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1802 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1802 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 1,378 items printed somewhere; 85 in 7 or more papers by the finder's count, 16 in 9 or more). Because the Treasury report, the proclamations of December 1801 and the acts of the session sit in families that began in 1801, the same script was also run with year 1801 over the 1802 pages (items_from_1801.json: 171 items, 19 in 7 or more). The finder's counts are those of chains (it joins items printed together, and acts that share the enacting formula), so every item in 6 or more papers was read in this session (Claude, the session's own model; no second reader) and counted by its own words, and every item in 5 or more was checked by machine for further papers: about 220 words of its text were compared with every page of the year in both transcriptions, and every page that shared many of its word sequences was read. Each act of the session was counted by its own title followed by its enacting clause. Each chosen item and each candidate set aside was counted with phrase searches on all 2,968 pages of 1802 in both transcriptions (story_phrase_search.py, phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json); every hit was read.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1800, 1804, 1805, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months from January to December and the main kinds of news (Europe and St. Domingo; ships, trade and the Barbary states; American public life and government). Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed was chosen and the others were not, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01); the Barbary items were trimmed as in 1804 and 1805. Every story alike (the owner's rule of 11 November 2026): no item was left out for its subject. Where several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story. A group count is a target, not a quota.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: Papers, not catalogue numbers, are counted (C-04): Jenks's Portland Gazette (sn83016063 to 20 September, sn83016072 from 27 September: Number 230 and 231 of Volume V), the Recorder of Richmond (sn84024678 to 27 October, sn84024679 from 3 November: the same printers, Pace and Callender) and E. Russell's paper at Concord, New Hampshire (sn84022876, the Republican Gazette, to 3 August; sn90062293, the American Republican Gazette, from 10 August) are one paper each. The 14 catalogue series of 1802 are 11 papers.

counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder chains the acts of the first session of the Seventh Congress through their enacting formula and the list of acts (items of up to 9 papers and 96 printings). Counted by its own title followed by its enacting clause, no act reaches 9 papers and three reach 7: the act fixing the military peace establishment (admitted), the act for the apportionment of Representatives and the act establishing a uniform rule of naturalization (not chosen). Five papers printed nearly every law (the National Intelligencer, Kentucky Gazette, New Hampshire Gazette, Rhode-Island Republican and Republican Ledger); the Oracle, the Portland Gazette, the Alexandria Advertiser and the Virginia Argus printed some. Pages that mention an act in the proceedings, or recite it in another act, are not counted.
counted_item_by_item.Thomas Paine's letters to the citizens: The finder makes items of single paragraphs of Paine's letters (up to 10 papers). Each letter is counted by its opening (C-06): the first letter is in 9 papers (the American Republican Gazette's printing of 7 December has its opening in print and in the CA text; RevX leaves it out), the second in 8, the third in 6 and the fourth in 6. Pages that quote passages in commentary are not counted (C-07): the Recorder's comments of 1 and 8 December, and the Alexandria Advertiser's reprint of them; the Kentucky Gazette's quotation of the first letter's last paragraph on 30 November; the Recorder's 'Extract from Paine's second letter' of 15 December; the Portland Gazette's quotations of the second and third letters. The passage on a 'female literary correspondent' that the first letter quotes also stands in Paine's letter to George Washington of 1796, which the Alexandria Advertiser reprinted in November; it is not counted with the first letter.
counted_item_by_item.The President's letter to Thomas Paine: Counted by its opening: 8 papers. A page that prints the letter whole counts, even inside an essay or among other letters, and the Alexandria Advertiser (12 October) and the Portland Gazette (6 December) printed it a second time (C-08); pages that quote part of it do not count (C-07): the Rhode-Island Republican's essay 'Seventy-Five, No. VI' of 25 September quotes only its first sentence, and the Alexandria Advertiser (16 October) and the Oracle (20 November) quote it from its second sentence.
counted_item_by_item.The committee's report on the public mon: The report of the House committee appointed 'to enquire and report whether monies drawn from the Treasury have been faithfully applied' (April 1802) is chained by the finder into items of 9 papers. By its opening it is in 6 papers (National Intelligencer, Alexandria Advertiser, Republican Ledger, Kentucky Gazette, Republican Gazette, Oracle); the Recorder and the Rhode-Island Republican printed extracts from its later parts, which are not counted (C-06); the Virginia Argus and the National Intelligencer's 'History of the last session' summarise it (C-07).
counted_item_by_item.The Treasury report of December 1801: The Secretary of the Treasury's report of 18 December 1801 on the finances was printed in parts in January 1802; the finder makes items of its paragraphs. By its opening it is in 7 papers on 1802 pages (the National Intelligencer printed it in December 1801). Later pages that quote its figures (the National Intelligencer and the Virginia Argus in August and September) are not counted. The page of the National Intelligencer filed under 29 November that opens with the same formula is the issue of 29 December 1802 and prints the next year's report.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item in two wordings or translations counts as one (C-02): the Consuls' proclamation to the inhabitants of St. Domingo (4 and 3 papers: 'you are all Frenchmen ... But an entire change has taken place', and 'ye are all Frenchmen, ye are all free ... But all is changed'), General Leclerc's proclamation of 8 June (6 and 3), the French Senate's address to the First Consul for life (5 and 3), the New York report of the fire of 2 November (5 and 2), and the New York report of the Algerine cruisers (7, and the Virginia Argus's Philadelphia form, which opens in other words and goes on in the same).
counted_item_by_item.Items printed together: Where one paper printed several documents in one column, each is counted by its own words: the Consuls' proclamation to the inhabitants of St. Domingo (7) and General Leclerc's own short proclamation that precedes it in several papers (5); the French Senate's address (8) and the First Consul's reply printed with it; the President's letter to Paine and letters of his to Callender printed in the same column of the Portland Gazette.
counted_item_by_item.Lists of the yeas and nays: Lists of members' names in the votes of the House (the finder joins several votes of February to August into one item of 7 papers) are parts of the proceedings, not items.
counted_item_by_item.Standing notices and advertisements: The Postmaster General's proposals for carrying the mails (6 papers, 54 printings in successive issues) and a commission of bankruptcy against a trader (a legal notice, 6 papers by the finder's count) are advertisements; neither reaches 7 papers.
